newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Kabul a city in turmoil as battle looms.
newsitem.headline: Kabul a city in turmoil as battle looms.

text.p: - Afghanistan's latest war is inching closer and closer to Kabul and many of its people are thoroughly fed up with the factional battles for power that have hurt them so badly.

"Why can't these people sit down and work out a deal instead of using guns that are going to kill us," wailed one market trader, an ethnic Pushtun like the purist Islamic Taleban militia now controlling the capital.
"We've had Masood, we've had Dostum, now we've got the Taleban. Life is miserable under all of them. Please, will someone give us a government we can live with," said one despairing intellectual.

The largely ethnic Tajik forces of ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, backed by northern Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum, are closing in on a city taken just three weeks ago by the Taleban.

Daily reminders of the danger facing a city bearing the widespread scars of battles for control during the past four years erupt spasmodically as Taleban fighters let loose with anti-aircraft fire for no discernable reason.
Bustling markets pause as the gunfire rings out, people wondering whether the latest battle for Kabul has begun.
So far, they have turned out to be false omens, but each burst is a harbinger, many Kabulis believe.

Since a Moscow-backed communist government collapsed in 1992 and a mujahideen guerrilla administration took over amid major battles between the various groups -- after 13 years of war that largely spared the city -- Kabul has known little but trauma.
Dostum and Masood were allies then. They fell out two years later when Dostum tried a coup, failed and withdrew to the north beyond the Hindu Kush.

"The Uzbeks treated Kabul like conquerors. They looted us, they kidnapped women for brothels. You think we want them back again," said the intellectual. "And Masood's men were corrupt like you wouldn't believe."
For many ordinary people, especially Pushtuns, the arrival of the Taleban and their imposition of Islam's stern Sharia law was a sublime relief.
"They don't allow corruption, they pay for what they want and we have peace and order," said one Pushtun trader.

But thousands of educated Kabulis fled Afghanistan's most liberal city when the Taleban ordered women to stay at home and appear on the streets only if clad in a burqa, an all-embracing veiled garment.
Taleban fighters, mostly from a countryside long ruled by mullahs (Islamic priests), enforced the edict by beating women they deemed improperly clad.

Three weeks later, there are few such incidents and the number of women on the streets has increased a little, "because our ladies have got used to the rules, even if they hate them", one male office worker said.
But most schools are still closed. Teachers conduct classes only in subjects such as mathematics and sciences because "the Taleban have problems with the syllabus", one parent said.
And outside the markets, Kabul's streets are still eerily quiet.
"In the summer, you couldn't drive easily through the streets of central Kabul, there were so many people," said one Western aid worker.
"The noise of the traffic used to wake me at six o'clock. Now I sleep till eight."
It is not only the Taleban edicts which scare Kabulis. Many Tajiks are afraid.

"You never answer the door after dark because it may be the Taleban coming to get you," said one who repeated oft-told stories of young men picked up to be sent to the front, even to be used as human mine-detectors.
The Taleban say some Masood sympathisers have had their houses searched for weapons and some have been arrested. But there is no evidence that men have been rounded up and sent to the front.
"I don't care what they say, we're all scared and if I could get out of Kabul, I would," said one Tajik man who said he had no money and no relatives outside the city to help.
"But the real problem is that nobody knows what is really happening or what's going to happen. That's why we're all scared."
